revision_notes: Light check surfaced substantive evidence, so this row was moved to the full path rather than confirmed as Unknown. Inflect.com (data-centre industry directory, Sept 2025) reports zero direct cloud on-ramps for AWS/Google Cloud/Azure in Malawi; enterprises reach hyperscale cloud via the Johannesburg regional hub, with AfriCloud reporting ~112ms latency Johannesburg-to-Blantyre — consistent with 'served remotely from distant regions only'. Newer local providers (Korena, a self-described Tier III+ 'sovereign AI cloud' in Blantyre; Sparc Systems' new Lilongwe data centre), both launched in 2026, claim in-country cloud/hosting capability, but these are self-published, promotionally worded claims from very new ventures (a competing firm separately claimed to be building Malawi's 'first' AI data centre in Feb 2026), so they were not treated as sufficient to move the score to 3 or 4. Recommend human review as the local cloud market is evolving quickly and claims could not be independently corroborated.
revised_comments: No major hyperscale cloud provider (AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud) maintains a direct point of presence or availability zone within Malawi; enterprises typically reach cloud services via the Johannesburg regional hub, with measured latency of roughly 110 milliseconds. A small number of local data-centre operators, including a newly launched sovereign cloud facility in Blantyre and a commercial data centre in Lilongwe, offer in-country hosting and GPU cloud services, though these are early-stage ventures not yet independently verified as full regional cloud availability zones.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.

revision_notes: Light check surfaced a clearly authoritative source, so this row was moved to the full path. Malawi enacted the Data Protection Act, 2024, which establishes the Malawi Data Protection Authority as an independent statutory body, with the Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority (MACRA) designated to oversee implementation. Score raised from 0 to 4 (legislation enacted with Data Protection Authority established). No evidence yet of an established enforcement track record or regional alignment, so 5 (mature framework with active enforcement) is not warranted.
revised_comments: Malawi has enacted comprehensive data protection legislation, the Data Protection Act, 2024, which establishes the Malawi Data Protection Authority as an independent statutory body responsible for safeguarding personal data and privacy, with the Malawi Communications Regulatory Authority (MACRA) designated to oversee its implementation.

Definition: Percentage of national population with access to electricity (grid or off-grid). This is the primary indicator of energy infrastructure availability for ICT. Based on World Bank/IEA Tracking SDG7 data, national statistical offices, or Afrobarometer surveys.
Comments: World Bank indicator page did not expose numeric values in fetched content; needs alternate extraction via API/download.
redteam_note: No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: The originally cited World Bank indicator page was fetched but its dynamic content did not expose the numeric value directly. Verified via the same World Bank/ESMAP SDG7.1.1 Electrification dataset mirrored on Trading Economics and CountryDataHub: Malawi's population access to electricity was 15.6% in 2023 (up from 14.0% in 2022). This is internally consistent with the same dataset's rural rate of 6.1% and urban rate of 57.8% (both 2023) once weighted for Malawi's largely rural population, giving confidence in the figure. Note: a separate 2026 World Bank 'Mission 300' National Energy Compact document cites a higher baseline of 25.9%, using a broader Multi-Tier Framework household-survey methodology that counts additional off-grid tiers (e.g. solar lanterns); this is a different metric from the standard WDI/SDG7 series specified in the metadata guidance and does not change the code here.
revised_comments: Malawi's national access to electricity rate stood at 15.6% of the population in 2023 according to the World Bank/ESMAP SDG7 electrification tracking dataset, one of the lowest rates in Sub-Saharan Africa, reflecting a stark urban-rural divide of 57.8% urban versus 6.1% rural access in the same year.

revised_comments: Malawi has an established off-grid and distributed energy policy framework under the National Energy Policy (2018), implemented through the Malawi Rural Electrification Programme and Rural Electrification Fund, with active but uneven deployment: a 2024 study identified 19 mini-grid installations with a combined 26 megawatts of capacity, alongside continuing World Bank-supported feasibility work on further sites, though several existing mini-grids have been abandoned owing to financial and regulatory challenges.

revision_notes: Light check surfaced strong, current evidence of severe outages, so this row was moved to the full path. ESCOM (the national utility) has published ongoing scheduled load-shedding programmes and, as of November 2025, was implementing near-daily load shedding across morning, midday and evening peak hours because of a persistent generation shortfall, with unplanned load shedding also triggered by hydropower station maintenance and reduced solar/hydro output. Historical World Bank Enterprise Survey data (via IndexMundi) already showed 6.7 outages per month for firms in 2014. Score of 1 (severe: frequent daily outages/regular load shedding) reflects documented current conditions.
revised_comments: Malawi experiences severe and frequent power outages, with the national utility ESCOM implementing near-daily scheduled load shedding during morning, midday and evening peak hours because electricity generation persistently falls short of demand; unplanned outages also occur when hydropower stations require maintenance or when reduced rainfall or cloud cover affects hydro and solar generation.
